title: V Foundation for Cancer Research Wine Celebration raises $6.87 million - The Napa Valley Register
content:
The V Foundation for Cancer Research Wine Celebration team celebrates $6.87 million raised at the 2026 event. The V Foundation for Cancer Research announced that its 28th annual Wine Celebration, held July 30 to Aug. 2 in Napa Valley, raised $6.87 million to advance cancer research. Since its start in 1999, the signature event has generated more than $188 million in support of the V Foundation's mission, according a news release. More than 350 guests, partners and philanthropic leaders gathered throughout the weekend “to support V Foundation grants awarded to top scientists and groundbreaking cancer research projects nationwide,” said the news release. The V Foundation has awarded more than $37 million through 102 grants to researchers and institutions across the San Francisco Bay Area. In total, V Foundation has eclipsed the $500 million milestone across nearly 1,500 game-changing cancer research grants, said the release. "The Wine Celebration is so much more than a beautiful weekend in Napa Valley,” said Brandi Williams Broome, CEO of the V Foundation. “For 28 years and counting, it's been a driving force behind the V Foundation's mission and the extraordinary progress we've made together. Because of the unwavering generosity of our dedicated supporters, vintner partners, and the entire Napa Valley community, we’ve been able to fund the bold science that gives families more time, more hope, and more answers.” You can reach reporter/business editor Jennifer Huffman at 707-256-2218 or jennifer.huffman@napanews.com Keep it Clean. title: Relight Gaussian splats with V-Ray 7, update 4 - Jon Peddie Research
content: Real-time rendering now also available in almost all major DCC applications. The latest V-Ray 7 does not carry a new release number but rather a new update figure. Nevertheless, the added  features and capabilities speak for themselves, making this offering significant. V-Ray 7, update 4 makes real-time rendering available in a multitude of digital content creation applications and, among other things, introduces the first way to relight fully ray-traced Gaussian splats. Chaos V-Ray 7, update 4 enables relighting of Gaussian splats. (Source: Chaos) At Siggraph 2026, Chaos hosted a full day of talks, live demonstrations, and conversations centered around rendering, visualization, AI, and digital production. The day prior, the company kicked off the conference by announcing V-Ray 7, update 4, making real-time rendering with path-traced feedback available directly in almost every major DCC application’s viewport—without exporting assets to a separate game engine. So, from the start of a project, users get instant, path-traced feedback right where the artist works, without any tool switching, fewer conversions, and less rebuilding when working on their V-Ray scene. The workflow is available through a Vantage Hydra Delegate for Houdini and an enhanced Maya Live Link, with 3ds Max integration introduced earlier this year. Support for Blender is coming soon via Live Link; Chaos is also developing an OpenUSD Hydra Delegate to bring Vantage’s real-time and V-Ray’s offline rendering into other host applications, including Nuke and Katana. “Artists lose time when a scene has to be converted or rebuilt when it moves between tools,” said Allan Poore, chief product officer at Chaos. “V-Ray 7, update 4 keeps the same asset moving from early exploration to on-set production and final rendering. That means faster feedback, fewer technical interruptions, and more time to focus on the shot.” With this update, users also can relight fully ray-traced Gaussian splats for blending scanned, real-world environments into 3D scenes. Because scanned environments usually include baked-in lighting that’s part of the original capture image, it becomes difficult to match the lighting to a 3D scene. Gaussian splat relighting, however, allows artists to adjust the lighting of captured environments in Houdini, Maya, 3ds Max, and Vantage (and coming soon to Blender) without re-creating the location or using complex workarounds. Additionally, the release expands Chaos Arena’s real-time toolset for virtual production with new features such as real-time material editing, real-time depth of field, decal color corrections, and lens encoder support. According to Chaos, V-Ray 7.4 delivers faster CPU and GPU rendering—GPU interactive previews can now begin up to twice as fast, while CPU rendering is up to 13% faster on supported configurations. V-Ray 7.4 is available now, extending across Maya, 3ds Max, Blender, and Houdini. WHAT DO YOU THINK?  LIKE THIS STORY? TELL YOUR FRIENDS, TELL US. title: Three quarter-final berths still up for grabs at Romania 2026 - IHF
content:
After the opening day of the main round at the 2026 IHF Women's Youth World Championship, five quarter-finalists have already been confirmed, as Egypt, Denmark, Spain, Montenegro and the People's Republic of China are all certain to progress. However, three spots are still up for grabs, and the final main round matches on Tuesday 4 August will complete the quarter-final line-up. The group stage of the President's Cup will also conclude with eight encounters, and Tuesday's matches will determine which teams remain in contention for the consolation trophy. MAIN ROUND
Group I
11:45 EEST — Egypt v Denmark
14:00 EEST — France v Republic of Korea Group II
16:15 EEST — Spain v Montenegro
18:30 EEST — Germany v Netherlands Group III
16:15 EEST — Hungary v People's Republic of China
18:30 EEST — Sweden v Romania Group IV
11:45 EEST — Slovakia v Switzerland
14:00 EEST — Japan v Slovenia PRESIDENT'S CUP
Group I
16:15 EEST — Croatia v Czechia
18:30 EEST — Republic of Fiji v Mexico Group II
16:15 EEST — Guinea v Portugal
18:30 EEST — Uzbekistan v Argentina Group III
11:45 EEST — Tunisia v Kazakhstan
14:00 EEST — Canada v Uruguay Group IV
11:45 EEST — Brazil v Serbia
14:00 EEST — Angola v Algeria After three victories in as many group matches, Switzerland extended their winning run in their first main round game, beating Japan 41:31. Line player Cristina Hofstetter became their top scorer in that encounter with eight goals, while left wing Lauryn Mierzwa, who scored seven times, is currently the joint top scorer of the tournament with a tally of 35 goals. With four points and sitting top of Group IV, the Swiss team are already certain to achieve their highest-ever finish at the IHF Women's Youth World Championship, improving on their 14th-place finish at China 2024. With a win or a draw against Slovakia, Switzerland will secure a place in the quarter-finals—and they could even progress with a defeat, depending on other results. Slovakia, who also claimed maximum points in the preliminary round, opened the main round with a narrow 23:24 defeat against Slovenia, conceding the decisive goal just seconds before the final buzzer. Sitting on two points, they still have a chance of reaching the quarter-finals, but will most likely need a victory over Switzerland to keep that dream alive. Both quarter-finalists from Group I have already been decided, and now Egypt and Denmark will meet in a direct battle for first place. The winner will maintain a perfect record at Romania 2026 and finish top of the group, while Egypt would also secure first place with a draw thanks to their superior goal difference. Egypt, the surprise package of the tournament, confirmed their ambitions at the start of the main round. After defeating Croatia, France and the Republic of Fiji in the preliminary round, they produced a dramatic comeback against the Republic of Korea. Trailing by six goals with just seven minutes remaining, the African side mounted a remarkable fightback to claim another two points. Denmark also had to work hard for their victories in the preliminary round, winning two of their three matches by a single goal. On Monday, they added another narrow victory, defeating France 21:19. Goalkeeper Thilde Ladegaard Skov delivered an outstanding performance with 15 saves and a 44% save efficiency, and if she produces another display of that calibre on Tuesday, Denmark will have every chance of ending Egypt's impressive run. Like Group I, both quarter-finalists from Group II have already been determined, with Spain and Montenegro level on four points. Both European sides still boast perfect records at Romania 2026, but only one can preserve it after their head-to-head clash, which will decide the group winner. Spain, the reigning champions, are determined to defend their title and have lived up to expectations so far. After victories over Guinea, Uzbekistan and Germany in the preliminary round, the Iberian side overcame the Netherlands 30:26 thanks to a strong second-half performance, securing a place in the last eight. Montenegro, who finished 18th and 12th at the previous two editions of the competition, are now guaranteed to improve on those results. The bronze medallists at the W17 EHF EURO 2025 have yet to drop a point, and a hard-fought 27:26 victory over Germany on Monday secured their place in the quarter-finals. Both teams will be eager to finish top of Group II in the hope of facing a more favourable opponent in the knockout stage. Spain hold a superior goal difference (+7 compared to Montenegro's +2), meaning a draw would be enough for them to finish first. Hungary rescued a dramatic 24:24 draw against hosts Romania with a late comeback, and despite dropping their first point of the tournament, they remain well placed to reach the quarter-finals. The two-time defending bronze medallists sit second in Group III with three points. The Hungarians will guarantee progression with either a win or a draw on Tuesday. Even a defeat could still be enough, but in that scenario they would need Romania to fail to beat Sweden. Meanwhile, the People's Republic of China have already made history at Romania 2026 by securing their first-ever top-eight finish. By defeating Sweden in their opening main round match, the Asian side proved that their perfect preliminary-round record was no coincidence. China's standout player, Shuoyan Zhang, was once again in outstanding form, scoring 13 goals against Sweden to move level at the top of the tournament scoring charts with 35 goals. The left back will be looking to add to that tally against Hungary. A draw would be enough for China to finish top of the group, while a Hungarian victory would see them leapfrog the Asian side into first place. title: The Ongoing Storm Rule Just Got Narrower- What Gallardo v. Walmart Means for New Jersey Slip and Fall Claims - The National Law Review

Winter slip-and-fall cases are among the most common premises liability claims in New Jersey, but they have also become some of the most difficult to litigate since the New Jersey Supreme Court adopted the “ongoing storm rule” in Pareja v. Princeton International Properties in 2021. On July 30, 2026, the Supreme Court issued its first significant interpretation of Pareja in Gallardo v. Walmart Stores, Inc. In a closely divided 4-3 decision, the Court held that Walmart could not be held liable for injuries sustained by a customer who slipped during an active winter storm, further narrowing the circumstances under which commercial property owners may be liable while precipitation is still falling. The decision is important not only because of its result, but because it answers one question left open by Pareja, while raising several others that will likely be litigated for years to come. In Pareja, the Supreme Court adopted what has become known as the ongoing storm rule. The rule recognizes that commercial property owners generally have no duty to continuously remove snow and ice while precipitation is actively falling. Instead, absent certain exceptions, they are afforded a reasonable amount of time after the storm ends to address winter hazards. The Court also recognized two exceptions to the rule: 1.) a commercial landowner may still owe a duty where its own conduct increases the risk to pedestrians or invitees by creating “unusual circumstances,” 2.) liability may exist where a dangerous condition predated the storm itself. However, Pareja did not explain was what exactly constitutes “unusual circumstances.” That unanswered question brought Gallardo to the Supreme Court. The case arose from a slip-and-fall in a Walmart parking lot during an ongoing winter storm. The storm started around 11:30 a.m. on January 3, 2016. Walmart’s snow removal contractor arrived at the store at 12:35 p.m. and spread salt on the lots and walkways until approximately 1:15 p.m. The contractor’s co-owner testified that when he got there, snow had not accumulated enough to warrant plowing. It is undisputed that Land Pros never pretreated the lot with salt or any other de-icing compound before the precipitation began. Approximately fifteen minutes after the contractor completed salting, the plaintiff slipped and fell. The plaintiff did not argue that Walmart failed to respond to the storm. Instead, her claim was that Walmart responded improperly. Her snow-removal expert opined that applying salt under those conditions, without pretreating or removing the accumulating snow, created an even more hazardous walking surface. In other words, the theory was not that Walmart did nothing. Rather, she asserted that Walmart’s remediation efforts actually made conditions more dangerous. That distinction ultimately became the central issue in the case. The procedural history of this case before the Supreme Court shows how genuinely close the the answer to this issue was. The trial court granted summary judgment to Walmart’s snow-removal contractor but denied Walmart’s motion. While the case was pending, the Supreme Court decided Pareja in June 2021, and Walmart moved for summary judgment a second time. The trial court denied that motion too, finding the first Pareja exception governed. Notably, the court’s articulation of the exception did not mention “unusual circumstances” at all. It framed the test as whether a commercial landlord’s actions increase the risk to pedestrians and invitees. A five-day trial followed. The trial court did not instruct the jury regarding the ongoing storm rule. Thereafter, the jury found Walmart negligent and found that negligence was the proximate cause of the fall. After the verdict was molded to account for past medical expenses and prejudgment interest was added, the trial court entered judgment for $1,328,658.59. Walmart appealed. The Appellate Division agreed with Walmart that the trial court committed error when it declined to instruct the jury regarding the ongoing storm rule. However, while the Appellate Division vacated the judgment and remanded for a new trial, it also held that Walmart was not entitled to summary judgment, judgment at trial, or judgment notwithstanding the verdict because, in its view, there was a genuine issue of material fact as to whether Walmart’s conduct made the parking lot more dangerous on the day of the accident. Both Gallardo and Walmart appealed. The Supreme Court denied Gallardo’s petition for certification and granted Walmart’s cross-petition. The Supreme Court reversed and directed that summary judgment be entered in Walmart’s favor. The majority concluded that Walmart’s conduct of spreading salt during an active storm did not constitute the type of “unusual circumstances” contemplated by Pareja. According to the Court, interpreting the exception to include ordinary snow-removal efforts, even if those efforts increase the risk of danger, would effectively eliminate the phrase “unusual circumstances” from Pareja altogether. Instead, the Court explained that both requirements must exist: the landowner’s conduct must increase the risk of harm, and the circumstances surrounding that conduct must themselves be unusual. To illustrate the point, the Court relied heavily on Terry v. Central Auto Radiators, a Rhode Island case previously discussed in Pareja. There, an auto repair shop required a customer to walk approximately one hundred feet across an unfamiliar, snow-covered lot to retrieve her vehicle during a storm. The Supreme Court concluded that the unusual circumstance was not failed snow removal, but rather the business’s affirmative decision to direct the customer into a hazardous area. The majority’s decision was driven largely by legitimate public policy concern. The Court expressed concern that exposing commercial property owners to liability whenever they attempted to salt, shovel, or otherwise remediate snow during an active storm would discourage those efforts altogether. If every unsuccessful snow-removal effort could become the basis for liability, property owners might simply wait until the storm ended before taking any action. The Court declined to create that incentive and instead interpreted Pareja narrowly, concluding that ordinary snow-removal efforts, even if later criticized as ineffective and/or danger increasing, are generally protected during an ongoing storm. One procedural issue also played a significant role in the Court’s analysis. Although the case proceeded to trial after Pareja was decided, the jury was never instructed on Pareja’s “unusual circumstances” requirement. Instead, the jury was asked only whether Walmart’s conduct increased the danger to pedestrians and invitees. The majority viewed that omission as significant because, in its view, the jury never decided the threshold question required under Pareja. For the same reason, the Court directed the Committee on Model Civil Jury Charges to revise Model Civil Jury Charge 5.20B, which currently focuses on whether the defendant increased the risk of harm but does not expressly include the “unusual circumstances” language. Justice Fasciale, joined by Justices Noriega and Hoffman, authored a comprehensive dissent that would have affirmed the jury’s verdict. The dissent first questioned whether Pareja should have applied at all. Specifically, because the plaintiff’s accident occurred years before Pareja was decided, the dissent expressed concern with applying a newly announced common-law rule retroactively. The dissent also questioned whether the ongoing storm rule should extend beyond public sidewalks to privately owned commercial parking lots, an issue the majority ultimately declined to decide. However, even assuming Pareja applied, the dissent concluded that the majority fundamentally misinterpreted the decision. In the dissent’s view, the majority transformed “unusual circumstances” into an independent hurdle that Pareja never intended. Instead, the dissent reasoned that the unusual circumstance is the commercial landowner’s affirmative conduct when that conduct increases the danger beyond what the storm itself created. Under that interpretation, whether Walmart’s snow-removal efforts actually made the parking lot more dangerous was precisely the type of factual question that should have remained with the jury. The decision unquestionably strengthens the ongoing storm rule for commercial property owners. Simply presenting expert testimony that snow-removal efforts were negligent, or even made conditions worse, will likely no longer be enough to survive summary judgment. Plaintiffs must now demonstrate not only that a defendant’s conduct increased the risk of harm, but also that the conduct occurred under “unusual circumstances.” While the decision clearly narrows the exception recognized in Pareja, it provides little guidance regarding what actually qualifies as an “unusual circumstance.” The opinion explains why Walmart’s conduct did not satisfy the exception but offers few examples of what conduct would. That uncertainty is likely to become the next battleground in ongoing storm litigation. Future cases will almost certainly focus on defining the boundaries of the exception and determining when a commercial property owner’s affirmative conduct crosses the line from protected snow-removal efforts to conduct that “unusual.” Gallardo represents one of the most significant New Jersey premises liability decisions in recent years. While the Court strengthened protections for commercial property owners responding to active winter storms, it also left important questions unanswered that will shape future litigation. For anyone injured in a winter slip-and-fall, one lesson remains unchanged: act quickly. Photographs, surveillance footage, weather records, contractor logs, and witness statements often become the most important evidence in determining whether a claim exists. As Gallardo demonstrates, the timing of the storm, and the property owner’s response to it, can determine the outcome of the entire case. title: Boilerplate or Not: Reading “Secure” Broader Than IPSec in MPH v. Apple - Patently-O
content:
The Federal Circuit today rejected a claim construction that had limited the word "secure" in MPH Technologies' patents to one particular protocol, IPSec.  The court then vacated the stipulated judgment of noninfringement. MPH Technologies Oy v. Apple Inc., No. 2025-1069 (Fed. Cir. Aug. 3, 2026) (nonprecedential). Judge Stoll's opinion separately reversed a holding that claim 1 of MPH's U.S. Patent No. 7,937,581 is indefinite. I see the case as asking something like "how much slack a patentee gets for imprecise drafting?" The district court had noted IPSec appears in the '949 patent close to 200 times, and the specification says that "[a]n essential idea of the invention is to use the standard protocol (IPSec)."  But, against all of that the panel set a single sentence near the end of the summary of the invention: "The invention is not restricted to the details of the figures and accompanying text, or any existing protocols, such as the currently standardised IPSec." The panel called the construction question "a very close issue" and held that the one sentence wins, noting that it was not simply boilerplate, but included the specific protocol by name. On indefiniteness, the district court treated a mismatch in antecedent basis as fatal, but the appellate panel found the scope reasonably certain. To continue reading, become a Patently-O member. title: Toyota RAV4 Needs A Hail Mary To Catch Honda CR-V As America's Favorite Car - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update The Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V are not the largest crossover SUVs available in the US market, but they do represent the largest annual sales volume. The RAV4 has dominated sales since 2017 – representing America's best-selling vehicle without a bed – while the CR-V had the lead from 2014 to 2016. This year, there's a good chance the CR-V will reclaim the sales crown, as Toyota has dealt with tight inventories and supply-chain disruptions as the all-new sixth-generation RAV4 has rolled out, since December. The good news for Toyota fans is the RAV4 is recovering. But the bad news is it might not be enough to stave off the CR-V's challenge. It's been a slow ramp up for the RAV4, impacted this year by war with Iran choking shipments of oil and other raw materials through the Straits of Hormuz for the auto industry, stranding more than 1,000 freighters and oil tankers as of last week. ​​​​​​ Plus, Trump administration tariffs of up to 25% on vehicles imported from Canada have dinged Toyota's North American profits, as most RAV4s for the US have come from Ontario plants in Woodstock and Cambridge. As tariffs escalated, Toyota quickly scrambled to shift more RAV4 production to Georgetown, Kentucky, to protect profit margins on the automaker's best-selling vehicle. It was barely a month ago that production of the new RAV4 started in Kentucky. So now it's a race to Dec. 31 to see which SUV will be America's bestseller in 2026. Honda has a huge lead, having delivered 264,449 CR-Vs in the US through July, an increase of 8% over the same period in 2025. Meanwhile, Toyota has sold 185,240 RAV4s through July, representing a 33.7% dip from the same period in 2025. That's a gap of nearly 80,000 units to overcome in five months. Impossible? We'll see. But isolating sales just for the month of July should give Toyota and its dealers a bit of inspiration. Last month, Honda sold 38,335 CR-Vs in the US, up 18.8% from July 2025. Toyota, on the other hand, sold 31,285 RAV4s in July, down 21.3% from July 2025. For context, RAV4 sales in the US were down 48% in the first quarter to 21,693 units as the perfect storm of war with Iran and tariff pressures hindered the RAV4 launch. In that same quarter, Honda sold nearly 41,000 CR-Vs, so here's the takeaway: Toyota is closing the gap. Powertrain mix might also be a factor. At a time when volatile fuel prices are pushing shoppers into hybrids, Honda is capacity constrained for its CR-V hybrid, while every new 2026 RAV4 is a hybrid. Plug-in hybrid RAV4s are coming from Japan. But it's too early for Honda to celebrate reclaiming the sales crown with the CR-V, especially because Honda, like Toyota, also builds its midsize crossovers in Honda's Plant 2 in Alliston, Ontario, meaning those CR-Vs could be subject to tariffs as well. The upside for Honda, however, is that the automaker builds most CR-Vs for the US in East Liberty, Ohio; and Greensburg, Indiana, which nullifies tariff concerns. Even if Toyota continues a rapid production ramp-up of RAV4 in Kentucky for the next five months, the automaker will be hard-pressed to catch Honda and pass the CR-V, with its huge sales lead more than halfway through the year. After seven months, RAV4 sales are finally trending upward. But pent-demand can be a powerful thing, and there's lots of it for the all-new RAV4, as customers were told earlier in the year that it's best to place an order, rather than picking one off the lot at your neighborhood Toyota dealership. At one point this year, RAV4 inventory was "critically low," as thin as six days' supply. In metro Detroit, a quick check of local dealerships finds plentiful stocks of the new RAV4. title: V-22 Osprey: Inside Military Aviation’s Most Controversial Aircraft - The Defense Post
content: The V-22 Osprey was built to overcome one of military aviation’s longest-standing tradeoffs: helicopters can take off almost anywhere, but airplanes can travel farther and faster. By combining both capabilities in a single tiltrotor aircraft, the Osprey has carved out a unique role in troop transport, special operations, and expeditionary warfare. Its service history, however, has been shaped not only by its groundbreaking design but also by a series of accidents, technical challenges, and debates over cost and reliability. This guide examines how the V-22 was developed, how it works, where it has been used, and the issues that continue to influence its future. The V-22 Osprey is a tiltrotor aircraft jointly developed by Bell and Boeing. It combines the vertical takeoff and landing capabilities of a helicopter with the speed, range, and efficiency of a turboprop airplane. Unlike conventional helicopters, the Osprey’s engines and rotors are housed in rotating nacelles at the ends of its wings. These nacelles can pivot between vertical and horizontal positions, allowing the aircraft to transition between hover and forward flight. The innovative design has enabled capabilities unavailable to most traditional rotorcraft, but it has also been accompanied by technical challenges and a series of fatal accidents throughout its development and operational history. Those incidents contributed to the aircraft’s controversial reputation, with critics and some service members at times referring to it as the “widowmaker” despite its widespread adoption across multiple US military branches. The origins of the Osprey can be traced to the aftermath of Operation Eagle Claw, the failed 1980 US hostage rescue mission in Iran, which exposed the need for an aircraft capable of combining long-range, high-speed flight with vertical takeoff and landing. The requirement led to the launch of the Joint-service Vertical Take-Off/Landing Experimental program, from which the V-22 ultimately emerged. The aircraft made its first flight in March 1989, but translating its unconventional tiltrotor concept into an operational military platform required years of testing, engineering refinements, and validation. The extended development pushed the program well beyond its original timeline before the V-22 finally entered service with the US Marine Corps in 2007. This is the baseline production variant and the most numerous in service. Designed primarily for assault support, it transports Marines, equipment, and supplies during amphibious assaults, expeditionary operations, and humanitarian missions. The MV-22B has also accounted for the majority of operational Osprey mishaps, with 23 of the 35 fatal accidents recorded after the aircraft entered service. Despite this, its Class A mishap rate has generally been comparable to the Marine Corps aviation average over the same period, indicating that the platform’s safety record has improved considerably since its troubled development. Operated by the US Air Force Special Operations Command (AFSOC), the CV-22B is optimized for long-range special operations. It incorporates terrain-following radar, advanced navigation systems, enhanced communications, and additional fuel capacity for low-level infiltration, exfiltration, counter-drone, and personnel recovery missions. Twelve of the 35 post-service fatal Osprey mishaps have involved the CV-22B. However, its Class A mishap rate, approximately 11.55 mishaps per 100,000 flight hours, has remained substantially higher than the Air Force-wide average of 1.65 per 100,000 flight hours, contributing to continued scrutiny of the variant’s operational safety. Developed to replace the C-2A Greyhound in the carrier-onboard delivery role. The CMV-22B transports personnel, cargo, mail, and high-priority components, such as the F-35‘s Power and Thermal Management System, between shore bases and aircraft carriers at sea. It features extended-range fuel tanks and long-range communications tailored for naval logistics. The navy has reported that its variant has not experienced mishaps or fatalities. The Osprey’s defining feature is its ability to rotate its engine nacelles 90 degrees. During takeoff and landing, the rotors point upward like a helicopter. Once airborne, they rotate forward, enabling faster and more efficient airplane-like flight. Traditional helicopters often face tradeoffs between speed and lift. The V-22 reduces that compromise by combining vertical lift with cruise speeds significantly higher than most military helicopters. The aircraft’s folding wings and rotor blades allow it to operate from amphibious assault ships and aircraft carriers while minimizing storage space requirements. The V-22 made its combat debut in Iraq in 2007 before expanding operations to Afghanistan. Its combination of speed, range, and vertical-lift capability allowed US forces to move troops, equipment, and casualties over long distances while reducing transit times and limiting exposure to roadside threats. The aircraft became a key asset for assault support and special operations missions in both theaters. Japan became the first international operator of the V-22, acquiring the aircraft to strengthen rapid deployment and the defense of its remote islands. Stationed with the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force, the Osprey plays an increasingly important role in responding to regional contingencies and improving interoperability with US forces across the Indo-Pacific. The V-22 has expanded the logistical flexibility of US carrier strike groups by enabling faster, longer-range resupply missions across the Indo-Pacific and other theaters. Its ability to rapidly move personnel and mission-critical equipment between dispersed naval forces supports the navy’s shift toward more distributed maritime operations, where ships are expected to operate over greater distances while remaining combat-ready. More than three decades after its first flight, the V-22 remains the only military tiltrotor aircraft in large-scale operational service. New variants continue to expand its mission set, while lessons learned from the program are influencing next-generation vertical-lift aircraft such as Bell’s V-280 Valor. Although debates over cost, maintenance, and safety continue, the Osprey has demonstrated that tiltrotor technology can provide capabilities that neither traditional helicopters nor fixed-wing transports can fully match. As militaries place greater emphasis on speed, reach, and operational flexibility, the V-22’s legacy is likely to shape vertical-lift aviation for decades to come.

title: From the Archive: What Happens When You Stuff an M5 V-8 into an E46 3-Series? - Car and Driver
content:
How do you get eight into three? You crib the answer from Herbert Hartge—the mastermind behind this M3-bodied M5-engined monster. BMW's M5 is a fantastic car, but it has evolved over the years from a mid-size hot rod to a gentleman's express, becoming more, shall we say, lexurious in the process. Drivers wanting a more responsive, compact sports sedan might be better off looking at the M3. But the M5's V-8 engine still makes a very compelling argument. Okay, then, why not put the M5's V-8 into a 3-series body? That idea also occurred to Herbert Hartge, owner of a reputable BMW tuner company in Beckingen, Germany. So he started work on the conver­sions. They're so good that another BMW tuner—Racing Dynamics—is reported to have leased one of the half­-dozen existing H50s (Hartge's name for BMW's V-8-powered E46) from a cus­tomer and passed it off as RD's own product at the Essen auto show, using camouflaged pieces to disguise the car's origins. The car you see here is Herbert Hartge's personal H50, on brief loan to his company's local distributor, DAZZ Motor­sport, in Baldwin Park, California. DAZZ allowed us to test the car and run laps at the Streets of Willow at Willow Springs International Motorsports Park in Southern California, where it was soon apparent that this is a pretty immaculate conversion. See all results for used 2001 BMW M5 for sale near 23917 Shoehorning the M5's potent V-8 and six-speed manual into a BMW 3-series body is no mean feat. It's no longer than the original six, so the firewall remains untouched, but it is much wider—so much so that the steering column had to be routed through the left exhaust header spaghetti, and the oil circulation must pass through the left engine mount. Otherwise, it's a stock motor with a reprogrammed chip and a revised engine speed limiter that will allow the tach needle to spin to the far side of seven grand. Oops! Despite the M5 engine's famous torque spread and the car's lighter bodywork, this H50 runs shorter-than­ M5 gearing—a 3.15:1 axle vs. 2.81. We recorded a 4.5-second sprint to 60 mph and a quarter-mile time of 12.9 seconds at 113 mph, but achieving those num­bers required some deft footwork. The H50 smokes the rear tires if you drop the clutch with any kind of revs on the dial. To hook it up, we had to let in the clutch at little more than idle speed, and even then the car would still smoke the fat 265/30ZR-19 Pirelli P7000s if we went abruptly to full throttle. Then, if we shifted out of first gear too exuber­antly, the tires would spin well into second. All this with a fairly decent weight distribution of 53 percent up front and 47 percent in the rear. Are you getting the picture here? This car is strong—nearly 400 horsepower strong—and it has tons of torque available across the engine's range. On the Streets course, this translates into telescoped straights, where you find yourself threshold-braking even when you weren't planning to, just to get slowed down for the bends. See all results for used 2001 BMW M5 for sale near 23917 On the exit of those bends, any over­-enthusiasm on the part of your right foot will push this car into power oversteer. Yeahhh, baby! But it's not like the car is way loose or anything. On the contrary, it's set up tautly, with lowered and stiffened springs, firm shocks, and beefy bars, and it will understeer at the limit as its maker intended until you get on the loud pedal. It's actually pretty hard to be smooth in the H50 on a tortuous track like the Streets without serious self-restraint. Overdriving it is almost an automatic response until we realize the need to slow our inputs down to go faster. Then the H50 moves around the track with deadly force. Its taut control calibration feels very BMW-like, and the conversion has successfully cap­tured the essence of the Bavarian marque. That's not too surprising. Hartge has been undertaking conversion work on BMWs for quite some time, putting 5.0-liter versions of the 540 and 740 V-8s into Z3s, M coupes, and 3-series bodies, among other things. Practice makes perfect, and even with the many add-ons—there's a page full of body additions, interior trim pieces, replacement instrumentation, and tire-and-wheel combinations available in the Hartge catalog—the H50 looks just like a hot 3-series BMW should. For American customers, a local 328i or 330i is shipped to Germany for the con­version. The finished product will look something like a U.S-market BMW, but with whatever body kit and wheels you ordered. Twenty-inch wheels (requiring a 25-series rear tire) are available if you desire repeated visits to the wheel-straight­ening shop. Come to think of it, the H50 will probably never look terribly much like a U.S.­market BMW. The Hartge insignia and V-8 badges will give the game away immediately, even to those who fail to notice the James Earl Jones exhaust note. Not unexpectedly, the H50 is priced the way a hot aftermarket BMW usually is­—in this case, about $120,000. The good news is that the price includes the donor car. The bad news? title: Sony RX10 V review: the all-in-one travel camera - The Shortcut | Matt Swider
content: 🔭 24-600mm f2.8-4 Zeiss lens combines the 25x zoom range of 5-6 lenses into one 📸 Ideal travel camera for capturing both wide landscapes and zoomed-in street subjects. 🖼️1-inch Exmor 20.1MP sensor is mid-range in resolution ⚙️ Stacked Bionz XR processor speeds up processing and burst shooting 🎬 Sony’s fully modern video suite adds 10-bit 4:2:2 S-Log 3 and LUT support 🧠 AI-powered real-time AF subject recognition and autoframing features 🔋 New Z-battery delivers dramatically longer life than the previous W-battery ֎ Lens aperture starts narrowing after zooming to just 25mm ⌛ Nine-year-old sensor stumbles over narrow dynamic range The $2,299 Sony RX10 V is Sony’s most flexible camera ever, and that’s largely due to the incredible reach of its 24-600mm-equivalent f2.4-4 Zeiss Vario-Sonnar 25x zoom lens. That gives you the equivalent focal range of 5-6 lenses without having to lug all that gear around. Then that flexibility is bolstered by a 20.1MP 1-inch Exmor sensor that shoots up to 30fps bursts, a fully modern Sony AF system, and video standards including 4K 120fps capture, S-Log3, and the ability to import up to 16 LUTs. Unfortunately, the Sony RX10 V trips over some fundamentals, including image quality that lacks dynamic range and poor high-ISO performance. Its AF system, while amazing most of the time, can struggle when pushed to the max by a busy background, a fast-moving subject, pushing maximum zoom, or a combination of all three. Despite these key issues, I found myself consistently amazed by how well the Sony RX10 V handled every kind of shooting I threw at it with aplomb. From spontaneous birding to macro shots of food and wide landscapes, the RX10 V kept surprising me with its deft flexibility to capture anything. If you’re looking for the best hybrid bridge camera available, there’s no question it’s the Sony RX10 V. However, if you’re looking for impeccable image quality, you’ll be better off getting a camera with a larger sensor like the Sony A6700 with a wide focal range for the same $2,299 price. 🔭 Big zoom. The biggest draw and first thing you’ll notice about this camera is its 24-600mm f2.8 to f4 Zeiss lens. That 25x range allows me to capture wide shots of the landscape and then zoom almost a mile away to capture far-off landmarks. This makes the camera a fantastic travel companion, as it essentially combines three to four lenses into a single piece of glass. The Sony RX10 V lets you go from shooting wide landscapes to portraits, up-close macro shots, and then long-range wildlife and sports all with one lens and one camera. ֎ Variable aperture. Unfortunately, the Sony RX10 V’s big zoom lens has the downside of a variable aperture that starts shrinking from f2.4 after the tiniest increment of zoom at 25mm. At 103mm, the lens locks in at an f4 aperture for the rest of the focal range. It’s not a huge pain to work around, but if you tire of tweaking your settings around the aperture changing all the time, you can just set the aperture to f4. 🖼️ 20.1MP sensor with leaf shutter. The Sony RX10 V features a 20.1MP 1-inch Exmor image sensor that’s mid-range in resolution, but fully stacked for faster image processing and burst speeds. The stacked Bionz XR processor allows the RX10 V to capture images at up to 30fps. The leaf shutter also makes the RX10 V a fast shooter with flashes and speedlights thanks to high-speed flash sync. That said, the RX10 V’s high-speed flash sync isn’t the best implementation, as it’s limited to just 1/2000 sec, or 1/1000 sec with wider apertures, whereas the Fujifilm X100 VI’s leaf shutter can achieve up to 1/4000 sec high-speed flash sync. 📸 Good, but underwhelming image quality. Image quality from the Sony RX10 V is sharply detailed, but using effectively the same 1-inch sensor from nine years ago causes the RX10 V to falter in two ways. Editing any of the RX10 V RAW images in Sony’s Imaging Edge Desktop software reveals how narrow the dynamic range of this camera really is. I can barely change the highlights or shadows before the image starts graying out. Noise also starts overtaking images from the Sony RX10 V starting at ISO 1,600. Unfortunately, this is just one of the realities of using a 1-inch sensor. As of this review’s publication, both Adobe Lightroom Classic and Capture One haven’t added Camera RAW support for the Sony RX10 V, so we’ll be revisiting this review to see if it provides more latitude for editing images. 🎯 Hit Ratio. Sony’s latest Bionz XR processor and “AI processing unit” make the RX10 V’s autofocus system a mostly fire-and-forget affair. Once your subject has a tracking box around it, you can rely on this camera to capture it in sharp focus. That said, there were two scenarios where the RX10 V missed the mark, including tracking birds flying in front of an extremely busy background and subjects moving quickly towards me, and both happened while the camera zoom was maxed out. The Sony RX10 V isn’t as reliable as a true sports camera like the Sony A9 III – especially since it lacks Pre-Capture to start taking a continuous stream of photos with a half-pressed shutter – but it’s a great starting point for would-be amateurs. 🧠 AI chip. As with all of Sony’s modern camera releases, the RX10 V comes rocking an AI chip that powers everything from subject recognition to color reproduction and exposure control. The useful benefit is Real-Time Recognition AF, which can recognize and track a variety of subjects, including humans, animals, birds, insects, cars, trains, and planes. This AI chip also powers the autoframing feature from the Sony ZV-E1 I keep coming back to, and it’s even more useful with the Sony RX10 V’s long zoom lens to keep far away, moving subjects in the center of the frame. 🎬 Top video specs. The best upgrades from the RX10 V’s new Exmor sensor are that it features all of Sony’s modern video features, including S-Log 3 shooting at 10-bit and 4.2.2. Sony has also upgraded the movie recording resolution and speed with up to uncropped 4K60p and slightly cropped 4K120p. It also supports LUTs, so you can see how your footage will look at the start of your edit as you’re filming. The Sony RX10 V is the best bridge camera for video, and the fact that you can smoothly zoom to 25x just makes it even better. 📐 Modern redesign. Sadly, the RX10 V no longer carries the classic streamlined and hunched-down design of bridge cameras from the 2000s. Instead, Sony has updated this new version with a squared-off body and larger grip that mimics the dimensions and controls of the Sony a7 series. As a result, the RX10 V now features three separate dials and a large AF stick. The buttons on the top and back of the camera are also more pronounced. 🔋 50% more battery. The RX10 V didn’t get Sony’s latest batteries, but the Z-batteries promised 50% longer run times with up to 630 shots per charge; in my experience, I actually saw even better performance. After taking 250 photos, including shooting some 4K video, I only saw my battery life decrease by 25%. 📸 You’re looking for the best hybrid bridge camera available 🎒 You’re tired of carrying around multiple camera lenses 🎥 You’re looking for a travel camera with all the flexibility for video and photos 🖼️ You’re looking for impeccable image quality (get the Sony a6700 instead) 🌃 You shoot mostly at night and other dark environments (get the Sony a7S III instead) 🎞️ You want a camera for professional sports and nature photography (get the Sony A9 III instead) Kevin Lee is The Shortcut’s Creative Director. title: EDPB requests review of EU-US Data Privacy Framework following Trump v. Slaughter - IAPP
content: In light of the U.S. Supreme Court's decision over independent agencies, the European Data Protection Board is urging the European Commission to assess the ruling's potential impacts to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework. The European Data Protection Board has begun asking formal questions about impacts to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework stemming from the U.S. Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter decision on independent agency authority and oversight. The board sent a letter to the European Commission requesting it "closely assess" how the ruling might affect the U.S. Federal Trade Commission's posture and ability to uphold DPF commitments. "The EDPB wishes to highlight that the existence and effective functioning of one or more independent supervisory authorities in the third country, with responsibility for ensuring and enforcing compliance with the data protection rules, is one of the key elements to be taken into account when assessing the adequacy of the level of protection in a third country," EDPB Chair Anu Talus wrote to European Commissioner for Democracy, Justice, the Rule of Law and Consumer Protection Michael McGrath in the 31 July letter. Talus also noted the DPF's explicit references to FTC independence and a U.S. president's ability to remove a commissioner only for "inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office." The Supreme Court ruling runs counter to DPF independence commitments, with U.S. President Donald Trump removing former FTC Commissioner Rebecca Kelly Slaughter because he deemed her work to be "inconsistent with (the) Administration's priorities." The European Commission did not immediately respond to the IAPP's requests for comment on the matter. McGrath had not publicly raised concerns in the leadup to the Supreme Court ruling, noting in April the DPF was "mutually beneficial to both sides." "There is recognition in the U.S., and certainly there is on the European Union side that there is too much at stake to allow (the DPF) to slip," McGrath said. "We know that many large U.S. companies that are the direct beneficiaries of the DPF are on the same page as us in that respect." McGrath met with EDPB members during its June plenary, as noted in Talus' letter. Following that dialogue, the board held a more focused conversation on potential Trump v. Slaughter impacts at the July plenary. While the Commission ponders the EDPB's request, onlookers remain split on what the Trump v. Slaughter ruling actually means for the DPF. While standard contractual clauses and binding corporate rules would still be viable transfer mechanisms, a range of businesses continue to rely on the DPF for their EU-U.S. transfer needs. NOYB Honorary Chair Max Schrems, who spearheaded challenges that led to the invalidation of the DPF's two predecessor frameworks, told the IAPP "the deal is done" following the decision. He referenced a "clash at the constitutional level," with the ruling on independence creating a perceived breach of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, and potential political conflicts of interest as well. "The Commission is not a legal, but a political body. The approach under (European Commission President) Ursula von der Leyen was to just not provoke the irrational Trump administration. So while the situation seems legally obvious, the signals we get is that they will try to keep this topic under the rug until the (Court of Justice of the European Union) forces it back out." Schrems had been preparing the next legal challenge prior to the latest development, noting NOYB is "actively working on a lawsuit to put the matter back before the CJEU." There is a case to be made for a status quo approach to the situation, according to Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati Partner Maneesha Mithal, the former head of the Division of Privacy and Identity Protection at the FTC. During a recent IAPP LinkedIn Live, Mithal the FTC remains steadfast and "has not shown any retreat from commitments to enforce privacy process." "I think there's an argument that it wouldn't change those other forms of data transfers," she added. In a recent op-ed for the IAPP, University of Grenoble Alpes' Théodore Christakis, Georgetown University's Kenneth Propp and Alston & Bird's Peter Swire, CIPP/US, offered their analysis of why data transfers do not stand nor fall with FTC and how Trump v. Slaughter does not apply equally to the DPF's redress mechanism. This content is eligible for Continuing Professional Education credits. Please self-submit according to CPE policy guidelines. Tuesday’s RSL Leagues Cup contest on Apple TV features Max Bretos and Brian Dunseth on the primary English-language call, with Jorge Perez-Navarro and Marcelo Balboa providing the Spanish-language analysis. Media members looking to receive the document as an attachment or have further questions are asked to please contact RSL Communications via email at RSLcommunications@RSL.com. Despite the recent spate of winless matches, RSL remains in fifth place in a tightly-packed MLS Western Conference with 17 games remaining in its 22nd all-time MLS season, with Tuesday’s match three weeks removed from a 4-1 home exhibition win over English Championship side Burnley FC. The first of at least four international clubs to arrive on the Wasatch Front during a 30-day midsummer span, Burnley was denied early by a sixth-minute penalty-kick save from 2025/26 “Iron Man” and Captain Rafael Cabral, later buoyed by a brace from rookie FW Sergi Solans, the Club’s co-Golden Boot leader with Utah native and teenage MLS All-Star Zavier Gozo, who also added a goal and an assist on the night. Iconic RSL player Diego Luna converted a late penalty to determine the final margin, with Burnley becoming the 33rd different international opponent to compete on Utah soil against Real Salt Lake, which now boasts an all-time 18W-10L-7T mark against international visitors. The former U.S. Men’s National Team World Cup standout (2002, 2006), MLS Cup Champion (2010) as a player, and former Colorado Rapids manager (2014-16) has averaged 1.60 points per game with RSL in his 202 matches at the helm. Only Cup-winning former manager Jason Kreis (2007-13) – now the Club’s President of Soccer – boasts more games, more wins and a higher PPG average than Mastroeni in RSL’s 22 seasons. During the Mastroeni era, resilience, grit and determination have served as trademarks for RSL, with the Club suffering back-to-back losses on just 20 occasions in those 202 games. Saturday at St. Louis marked the latest opportunity for the Claret-and-Cobalt to display its “xDAWG” mentality as it earned the result at Energizer Park, previously winning 35 and drawing 17 times in “bounce-back” games following a loss in Mastroeni’s five-plus seasons in Utah. Real Salt Lake enters the tourney ranked as the 30th overall side out of 36 participants based on its 2025 performance and standings results, with RSL fifth of the six teams in the West 1 pod, which also includes MLS sides Vancouver and Minnesota, in addition to RSL’s three Liga MX opponents. Further information on each match can be found at www.RSL.com or www.LeaguesCup.com. RSL’s history with TIGRES UANL is the most extensive of any Liga MX opponent, with RSL and Tigres squaring off for a fifth occasion later this year. Tigres ousted RSL from the Concacaf Champions League back in 2016, winning 2-0 at home before drawing 1-1 in Sandy. In July, 2019, RSL fell 0-1 to Tigres at home in what was then called the Leagues Cup “Showcase,” a match that is known for a cat running on the field in what was former RSL Head Coach Mike Petke’s final match with the Club. Tigres first visited Utah back in 2008, arriving for a friendly as part of the Xango Cup, RSL winning the game at Rice-Eccles, 1-0. Former RSL centerback Carlos Salcedo arrived in Utah from the Tigres academy more than a decade ago, while RSL sold former goalkeeper Lalo Fernandez to Tigres at a similar juncture. The club now moves to Mexico City yet again, with the famed Estadio Azteca becoming its new home. Mazatlan was formerly known as Monarcas Morelia before relocation in 2020 – entering this summer’s tourney as the second of three visitors to the Beehive State, arriving for the second Phase One match on Saturday, August 8 (kickoff time TBD). Interestingly, back in July, 2006, Morelia did defeat RSL by a 3-1 scoreline at its former Rice-Eccles Stadium home. Former RSL Academy, Real Monarchs and RSL forward and Park City, Utah native Sebastian “Bofo” Saucedo played 17 games for FC Juarez from 2023-25, scoring one goal. content:
Talent is everywhere, but opportunity is not. As the first publication to interview Byron V. Every member of the Genesys Works team believes in empowering young people with the skills, confidence, and access needed to succeed in tomorrow’s workforce. As Genesys Works continues expanding into new markets, its vision remains clear: create opportunities wherever talent exists. Garrett and his team embody the timeless belief that it takes a village to raise a child, ensuring that today’s students become tomorrow’s professionals, mentors, and leaders. title: Amicus Brief in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County - Reason Magazine
content:
Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent In the upcoming climate change case the Supreme Court should reject the industry and Trump Administration arguments for preemption-by-penumbra. This morning I filed an amicus brief in Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. In this case, likely to be argued in October, the Supreme Court will consider, among other things, whether the Clean Air Act or the Constitution preempt state-law claims seeking relief for injuries allegedly caused by climate change. As my prior blogging on the subject has indicated, I find the preemption claims to be without merit. (I have no opinion on the procedural jurisdictional issue, but recommend the briefs by Profs. Derek Muller and Ben Johnson for an idea of the issues there.) Accordingly, my amicus brief focuses on the preemption claims. Here is the summary of my argument: Global climate change presents many complex and intractable legal and policy questions. Assuming this Court has jurisdiction, the legal questions in this case are comparatively simple and straightforward. Nothing in federal law, let alone the Constitution, preempts state-law claims seeking relief from injuries allegedly caused or exacerbated by petitioners' conduct. At issue in this case is whether allegedly aggrieved parties, including subnational governments, may seek re-dress under state law from defendants otherwise subject to state court jurisdiction for harms allegedly caused or contributed to by petitioners' conduct. In order to succeed, plaintiffs will ultimately need to show that the dam-ages they allege were caused by actions taken by defend-ants, that such actions are within the jurisdiction of state courts, and that such actions may be the subject of tort liability under state law. Allowing this case to proceed does not allow any State to impose a universal rule on all fossil fuel producers, let alone on all greenhouse gas emissions around the globe. The fact that emissions "can-not be unmixed and traced," Pet'rs' Br. 28, may complicate plaintiffs' ability to prove their case, but it does not justify—let alone require—preemption of their claims. Petitioners charge that respondents' claims are barred because both the Clean Air Act and the Constitution categorically preclude any claims seeking redress for harms caused by interstate pollution. Yet neither the Clean Air Act nor the Constitution imposes such a rule. To the contrary, as this Court has long understood, such suits may proceed, subject to certain limitations, even if they are viewed as efforts to seek redress for interstate pollution subject to federal regulation. That the Clean Air Act may constitute a broad, "comprehensive" regulatory scheme does not mean that it preempts state-law efforts to seek remedies for the alleged harms caused by the accumulation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Like other federal environmen-tal statutes, the Clean Air Act was enacted against a back-ground of extensive and essential state-law environmen-tal protections, including those provided by common law causes of action. That the Clean Air Act was meant to supplement, enhance, and encourage state-level efforts, rather than supplant or preempt them, is evident from the text, history, and structure of the Act. It is also what this Court has recognized. The Constitution's structure provides no more basis for closing the courthouse doors on respondents' efforts to seek redress for the harms they allege. Federal common law may once have preempted state attempts to control interstate air pollution under state law, but federal common law has been displaced, and no longer serves that function. Nor does any constitutional provision or doctrine identified by petitioners provide a basis for wholly preempting state-law claims seeking redress for harms such as those alleged here. Petitioners' attempt to cobble together an argument for constitutional preemption rests upon penumbras and emanations from various constitutional provisions that cannot hold the weight of their pro-posed rule. That is insufficient. "There is no federal pre-emption in vacuo, without a constitutional text or a federal statute to assert it." Hencely v. Fluor Corp., 146 S. Ct. 1086, 1093 (2026) (quoting Puerto Rico Dep't of Consumer Affairs v. ISLA Petroleum Corp., 485 U.S. 495, 503 (1988)). And "[i]nvoking some brooding federal interest or appealing to a judicial policy preference should never be enough to win preemption of a state law." Virginia Uranium, Inc. v. Warren, 587 U.S. 761, 767 (2019) (lead opinion). State law—statutes, regulations, and common law court decisions—has played an essential role in this nation's history of environmental protection. Resort to state law should not be foreclosed merely because such claims threaten economically important interests or rely upon expansive theories of liability or attenuated chains of causation. If such suits are to be preempted, that is a job for Congress, not the courts. The Court should decline petitioners' invitation to craft a new constitutional rule that would categorically preclude States from seeking to use state law to address environmental problems that relate to interstate pollution. Environmental problems rarely respect jurisdictional lines. Yet this has never barred the application of state law to environmental concerns, nor foreclosed efforts by state policymakers and affected parties to utilize state law to redress environmental harms. The Constitution provides the federal government with ample power to direct climate change policy and limit or preempt inconsistent, ineffective, or ill-advised state laws. Such power may be exercised by the political branches, through the process of bicameralism and presentment. The power to adopt an unheralded, unprecedented, and unbounded rule concerning interstate environmental problems does not lie in this Court, and this is reason alone to reject petitioners' arguments. While I do not address the foreign affairs preemption argument, I find it even less persuasive than the arguments I address, largely because it is an argument without limit. The United States is not currently party to any treaty--or even an international negotiation--that even threatens to conflict with a potential damage award. The idea that such suits could nonetheless be preempted because the defendants are engaged in multinational conduct or because the atmosphere (like, say, the internet) is global does not change the analysis. Congress could certainly preempt this litigation on foreign affairs grounds and (at least under current precedent, i.e. Garamendi) executive branch action might also be relevant, but there is no action here by the political branches that could or should have such effect. I also do not address the First Amendment arguments raised in some of the top-side amicus briefs, largely because those questions are not before the Court. As I say in my brief, there may well be constitutional constraints on tort liability for marketing claims of the sort at issue here, but that's not an argument for preemption of these suits at the outset. I expect to blog more on some of the issues in this litigation (and perhaps some of the many amicus briefs filed). In the meantime, for those interested, here are my prior posts on this subject: NEXT: Schools Owe No Legal Duty "to Former Students to Investigate Allegations of Past Abuse," Jonathan H. title: Hennessey’s New Blackbird Hypercar Brings an N/A V-8, a Gated Stick Shift, and Exactly 0 Screens - roadandtrack.com
content: The successor to the Venom has its sights set on driver pleasure, not setting records. Hennessey isn’t quite done building Venoms, but the Texas-based carmaker already revealing its successor: the Blackbird. This new project is designed to be the driver-focused option amongst Hennessey’s wild array of vehicles, and it will be publicly debuted at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering on August 14. While the Venom GT and Venom F5 are pushing for record-breaking performance, the Blackbird puts numbers in the rearview, instead prioritizing driver involvement. To that end, it has a naturally aspirated 6.2-liter V-8, a gated six-speed manual, and rear-wheel drive. The engine is being developed with Ilmor Engineering; in case you’re unfamiliar, amidst a long history in motorsports and more, Ilmor has partnered with Chevy to develop and build its IndyCar engines since 2012, and partnered with both Chevy and Honda to build the new hybrid IndyCar powertrain in 2025. Hennessey says it’s targeting 800-850 horsepower from this 6.2-liter, but doesn’t supply any details about how it plans to achieve such a high output beyond a claimed 9000-rpm-plus redline. Despite numbers not being the point, the Blackbird will still have some mighty ones to brag about: Hennessey says the 0-60 mile-per-hour sprint comes in just 2.5 seconds, and the top speed will be 220 mph. A claimed sub-3000-pound dry curb weight should be a big help in achieving those numbers. The Blackbird will make use of a new, bespoke carbon tub, and carbon fiber bodywork galore also contributes to the low weight. Inboard suspension architecture is paired with adaptive dampers, and Michelin Pilot Sport Cup2 tires will wrap one of two wheel options Hennessey will offer. You’ll have both traction control and ABS, but that’s it as far as control systems go. As you probably already guessed, the Blackbird name is derived from the SR-71 Blackbird. The car’s design also pulls inspiration from the aircraft. Hennessey says the active vertical stabilizers you see deploy at 71 mph and sit at +/- 71 degrees. Another aircraft-derived feature is the quad exhaust exit design, which Hennessey says is meant to mimic the Bell X-1’s exhaust ports. Hennessey emphasized the Blackbird’s interior as one of the most important parts of the experience. As you can see from the photos, there are no screens at all inside. That was intentionally done to offer a back-to-basics, driving-focused environment that Hennessey hopes will be timeless in design. Some of the highlights are the exposed linkage for the gated shifter, large central tachometer, and focus on visibility. Hennessey also says it chose to use a physical ignition key. However much technology you want in the Blackbird is dependent on what you bring along — namely, your phone. Details are a little thin, but Hennessey says it has a “hidden” technology strategy such that you can still pair the phone with the car. From there, the Blackbird has a “Hennessey holster” that you place your phone in to use as the car’s infotainment center. Presumably, it will be in an accessible enough place to run navigation and control the audio system. Long-haul driving was a priority for Hennessey with the Blackbird, as it says great effort was put into NVH and comfort for road trips. The car even has space for two small carry-ons in the front trunk, in addition to rear luggage pods. In perhaps its most American move, the Blackbird has four cupholders, hopefully with enough space for a Big Gulp. If you want one of these Blackbirds, there will be a fairly lengthy wait. Hennessey says it’s targeting production from 2029-2030. The price is $2.5 million before options, and only 71 will be built. According to Hennessey, “more than two-thirds” of the production run are already spoken for, so as of this story’s publishing, you can still get your foot in the door. title: Celtic v Dundee – Scorers in consecutive seasons - Yahoo Sports Canada
content: The year 1318 hardly stands out as one of the most significant in world history, although those interested in the Scottish Wars of Independence may be interested in some events. But for Celtic this season, the numbers 13 and 18 could yet have real significance, not least the latter number. Callum McGregor of Celtic arrives at the ground ahead of kick off in the Celtic v AC Milan in a pre-season friendly at Celtic Park on July 25, 2026. (Photo by WM Sport Media/Getty Images) As we enter season 2026-27, Callum McGregor and James Forrest have their own scoring records to beat, and in Forrest's case, it would make club history. So far, Callum McGregor has managed to score in 12 consecutive seasons for the Celts. This puts him level with 1960s legends John Hughes and Stevie Chalmers, as well as Adam Mclean, a popular Celt in the World War One era. Should McGregor score this season – which is hopefully just a matter of when, rather than if – it will move him onto 13 seasons, level with Jimmy Johnstone and Sandy McMahon. This would make him joint tenth in Celtic's overall records. James Forrest of Celtic scores to make it Celtic 2-0 AC Milan during the Celtic v AC Milan in a pre-season friendly at Celtic Park on July 25, 2026. (Photo by WM Sport Media/Getty Images) But for James Forrest, an even bigger achievement awaits. The Ayrshire winger is currently in joint second place in Celtic's records (along with Bobby Lennox) having scored in 17 successive seasons. A goal this year would take him onto 18, level with Celtic hero Jimmy McMenemy. It would be yet another accolade for Forrest, who has already written himself into club legend. Celtic's transfer activity has eventually got going and there are different new faces available for selection by Martin O'Neill. But hopefully some well-known faces can also get on the scoresheet too. Tonight would be a great time for these famous Celts to reach 13 and 18 – and make history at the same time. So come on Calmac and Jamesy, let's get those goals as early as possible preferably this evening. Camilo Duran of Celtic celebrates scoring opening goal with James Forrest to make it Celtic 1-0 AC Milan during the Celtic v AC Milan in a pre-season friendly at Celtic Park on July 25, 2026. (Photo by WM Sport Media/Getty Images) While it's certainly possible it is perhaps more likely that the Dundee defence will have more to worry them with both Kasper Hogh and Camilo Duran both making their competitive debuts for Celtic this evening and no doubt starting a personal race to be Celtic's top scorer this season. title: First Look: The Hennessey Blackbird Is an 850-HP Manual Hypercar With Zero Screens - MotorTrend
content:
This hypercar skips hybrid or EV tech in favor of a screaming engine and a gated manual. Tired of porky hypercars filled to brimming with batteries, motors, screens, and computers constantly doing their gol-dangedest to drive the car for you? Well, Texas’ favorite son John Hennessey has got you covered with his third hypercar offering: the Hennessey Blackbird, of which only 71 will be built. See, the thing is heavily influenced by the retired Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird long-range, high-altitude, Mach 3+ strategic reconnaissance aircraft. Not only does the Hennessey Blackbird eschew hybridization and screens of any type, it also keeps things simple by doing without turbochargers and automatic gear selection. That’s right, this naturally aspirated hypercar features a row-your-own six-speed manual gearbox, complete with visible linkage. The controls are analog, and there’s even a physical insert-and-twist ignition key. The car does, however, include antilock braking and traction control to make the most of the grip provided by the Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires. The initial press release is conspicuously light on engine specifics. Beyond an 800–850-hp target and a redline exceeding 9,000 rpm, Hennessey says little about the Ilmor-developed 6.2-liter V-8's architecture. We'd wager it retains at least the bore spacing and basic dimensions of GM's small-block, though likely with bespoke cylinder heads—and perhaps even a DOHC valvetrain. (Ilmor has developed lots of engines based on that small-block, making it plausible that it retains GM spacing or other core dimensions to simplify manufacturing.) No torque specs are provided, but we’re promised the naturally aspirated engine—which Hennessey claims is the highest-revving and most powerful naturally aspirated road-car V-8—responds with uncanny immediacy. The Hennessey Blackbird is slated to feature a carbon-fiber tub clad in carbon-fiber bodywork, all of which is expected to keep “dry weight” under 3,000 pounds. The suspension is adaptive, utilizing inboard linkage-controlled springs and shocks. That shifter had better be mighty slick, because Hennessey is claiming a 0–60-mph time of 2.5 seconds and even the snappiest manual shifts tend to take about a quarter-second. Though, with a claimed top speed of 220 mph, first gear may well be tall enough to reach nearly 60 mph. While performance is impressive, it’s intended to serve the driving experience rather than defining it. Several design cues are inspired by the SR-71, including the long stance, disciplined surfacing, crisp body-side line, and particularly by the vertical stabilizers. These deploy to the 71-degree angle you see in the photos at precisely 71 mph. Did we already mention production is limited to 71 examples? The diamond-shape orientation of the four rear exhaust pipes is inspired by Chuck Yeager’s Bell X-1 aircraft—the first to achieve Mach speed flight. Other design influences include the Formula 1–inspired side pods and LMP1-inspired winglets. While the numbers are impressive, the Blackbird aims to be remembered more for the tactile experience of driving it—the sound, look, and feel of the controls are all intentionally tactile and memorable. Concessions to long-haul comfort include sound deadening, open visibility, and the adaptive suspension. There’s also space for two full-size carry-on bags in the frunk plus rear-quarter storage, in-cabin stowage, and ample passenger space with gullwing doors to ease getting in and out. And while there are no screens (nor any steering wheel buttons), there is a “Hennessey holster” designed to mount a handheld device, providing Apple CarPlay or Android Auto connectivity and  navigation. Hence technology is there where you need it but never dominates the driving experience. The Venom F5 is Hennessey’s hero-numbers car; this one is more about emotional engagement, touring, and beauty. Deliveries of Hennessey’s second clean-sheet model after the Venom F5 are expected in 2029 or 2030 at a price of $2.5 million before options (which include a Sky Glass  asymmetrical tapering roof inspired by—what else—the SR-71 canopy) a choice of two wheel designs, and likely a range of color and trim choices. Oh, and if you’re interested, hurry up: More than two-thirds of production has already been allocated ahead of its August 14 public debut at The Quail during Monterey Car Week in California. title: Raytheon installs first SPY-6(V)4 radar at Wallops Island, advancing USS Pinckney upgrade and Navy destroyer backfit programme - Defence Industry Europe
content: RTX’s Raytheon has delivered and installed the first SPY-6(V)4 radar array at the Surface Combat Systems Center on Wallops Island, Virginia. The installation advances the U.S. Navy’s Flight IIA destroyer modernization effort and its wider SPY-6 backfit program. The land-based site provides an open-water environment for evaluating the radar before shipboard installation. Testing will cover the radar’s dedicated power system and interfaces with the Navy’s combat systems. Initial testing is scheduled to begin later this year and continue through mid-2028. The work will support installation aboard USS Pinckney (DDG 91), the first destroyer selected to receive SPY-6(V)4. “By leveraging the Wallops test site, we’ll be able to integrate SPY 6(V)4 with its dedicated power system before it reaches the ship, reducing the amount of testing needed on DDG 91,” said Barbara Borgonovi, president of Naval Power at Raytheon. “That means less time in the shipyard, more time dedicated to the mission, and a smoother path for future backfit ships.” USS Pinckney is scheduled to be available for the radar upgrade from late 2026 through 2028. The Navy and Raytheon are using shore-based testing to meet that timetable and ease the transition to shipboard installation and operation. SPY-6(V)4 is one of four variants within Raytheon’s SPY-6 radar family. It is the only version designed specifically for installation on existing Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class destroyers. The Wallops effort involves the U.S. Navy, NASA’s Wallops team and industry partners. The program is intended to deliver the upgraded radar capability to the surface fleet while limiting testing requirements aboard individual ships. Other SPY-6 variants are already installed aboard two commissioned U.S. Navy ships. Eleven additional vessels have received the radar and are undergoing testing before commissioning. The Navy expects to deploy SPY-6 across more than 50 ships during the next decade. The radar family is designed to improve detection and defense against air, surface, ballistic-missile and electronic-warfare threats. Raytheon has invested $800 million to modernize its radar manufacturing facilities and increase production capacity. The company expects to double SPY-6 output by 2028, supporting long-term availability and lower costs for the Navy. title: News | RTX's Raytheon completes installation of first SPY-6(V)4 array at Wallops Island test site - RTX
content:
WALLOPS ISLAND, Va., Aug. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Raytheon, an RTX (NYSE: RTX) business, has delivered and installed the first SPY-6(V)4 radar array at Surface Combat Systems Center at Wallops Island in Virginia, marking a major milestone for the U.S. Navy's Flight IIA Destroyer modernization effort and the SPY-6 backfit program. The Wallops site, a land‑based test facility situated over an open-water environment, will support extensive testing of the radar and its power and combat system interfaces ahead of installation on USS Pinckney (DDG 91), the first ship to be backfit with SPY‑6(V)4. SPY-6(V)4 is one of four variants in the SPY-6 family of radars, and is the only variant designed to backfit Flight IIA Destroyers. Initial testing will begin later this year and continue through mid‑2028. "By leveraging the Wallops test site, we'll be able to integrate SPY‑6(V)4 with its dedicated power system before it reaches the ship, reducing the amount of testing needed on DDG 91," said Barbara Borgonovi, president of Naval Power at Raytheon. "That means less time in the shipyard, more time dedicated to the mission, and a smoother path for future backfit ships." DDG 91 is scheduled to be available for the SPY-6(V)4 backfit from late 2026 to 2028. The Navy and Raytheon are using the Wallops site to meet this tight schedule and ensure a smooth transition from maritime environment testing to shipboard installation and operation. The effort is a collaborative undertaking involving the Navy, the NASA Wallops team and industry partners, reflecting a strong government-industry partnership focused on delivering enhanced capability to the surface fleet. Other SPY-6 radar variants are already onboard two commissioned U.S. Navy ships and have been installed on 11 additional ships currently undergoing required testing in preparation for commissioning. Over the next decade, SPY-6 is expected to be deployed on more than 50 U.S. Navy ships, enhancing defense against air, surface, ballistic and electronic warfare threats. Raytheon's SPY-6 family of radars is built on more than a decade of design, testing and manufacturing experience and has been validated by successful performance at sea. The company has invested $800 million to modernize its radar manufacturing facilities and expand production capacity. With these upgrades, Raytheon is positioned to double SPY-6 output by 2028, helping ensure long-term availability and lowering cost for the Navy.
