title: 'Behind Every Successful Woman Is a Husband': Justice V Mohana - LawBeat
content: Justice V. Mohana addresses SCBA felicitation after Supreme Court elevation. "Behind every successful woman, there is a husband and an entire family," newly appointed Supreme Court judge Justice V. Mohana said recently, delivering an emotional account of her journey from a government school in Tamil Nadu to the country's highest court while crediting her husband, parents, teachers, mentors and the Bar for shaping her legal career. Speaking at a felicitation ceremony organised by the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) for five newly appointed Supreme Court judges, Justice Mohana said her elevation was the culmination of decades of support from those who stood by her both at home and in the profession. Also Read| Justice V Mohana At Madras Bar Association Event: "Overwhelmed, My First Event Post Becoming Supreme Court Judge" The felicitation function, held at the Auditorium in the Administrative Building Complex of the Supreme Court, honoured Justices Sheel Nagu, Shree Chandrashekhar, Sanjeev Sachdeva, Arun Palli and V. Mohana, who were recently appointed to the apex court. The event was attended by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, judges of the Supreme Court, Attorney General R. Venkataramani, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, SCBA President Vikas Singh, office-bearers of the Bar Association, senior advocates and members of the Bar. Describing the occasion as "a very emotional moment", Justice Mohana said she was standing before the very institution where she had grown as a lawyer. "This is the place where I grew up, where I honed my skills as a professional, where I got so much love and affection. This is the Bar which has actually promoted, encouraged me, and allowed me to grow my wings," she said. Justice Mohana thanked the Chief Justice of India and the members of the Supreme Court Collegium for reposing faith in her by recommending her elevation. She also paid tribute to her parents, particularly her mother, whom she described as the driving force behind her legal career. Also Read| Representation Of Women In Higher Judiciary "It is my mother's dream that has brought me here," she said, adding that she had never imagined that one day she would stand before the legal fraternity as a judge of the Supreme Court. Recalling her childhood, Justice Mohana said she studied in a government school where teachers supported her not only academically but also by providing essentials such as uniforms and geometry boxes whenever required. She later joined Government Law College, Coimbatore, as part of the first batch of the five-year law course introduced in Tamil Nadu between 1983 and 1988. She also fondly remembered that fellow Supreme Court judge Justice Kalpathy Venkataraman Vishwanathan was her classmate and said they belonged to that "proud batch". Justice Mohana narrated how she began her legal career under veteran civil lawyer M. Panchapakesan in Coimbatore, where she learnt the fundamentals of civil trial practice and the Civil Procedure Code before shifting to Delhi in 1992 on his encouragement. Reflecting on the early years of her married life, she recalled living in a modest barsati accommodation in Karol Bagh. She said seeing her March 1994 Supreme Court Bar Association membership form during the felicitation ceremony brought back memories of those days. Also Read| Criticize Government But Do Not Denigrate India As A Nation: Senior Advocate Harish Salve She said she had the privilege of working with several leading members of the Bar and had briefed the Attorney General for India in numerous matters, experiences that helped shape her professional journey before she was designated a Senior Advocate by the full court of the Supreme Court in 2015. Expressing gratitude to her juniors, Justice Mohana said they had stood by her throughout her career by meticulously preparing every case. She encouraged young lawyers to dream big, saying that if someone from Pollachi, Erode and Coimbatore could reach the Supreme Court Bench, the younger generation could achieve even greater heights. She also acknowledged the support of her siblings, noting that she was the eleventh among thirteen children, and thanked her in-laws, her son and even the caregiver who looked after him while she pursued a demanding legal career. Concluding her address, Justice Mohana said she hoped to justify the confidence reposed in her by discharging her judicial responsibilities with the continued affection and cooperation of the Bar and the guidance of her brother and sister judges. "I am hopeful that I will be able to do the duty that has been given to me," she said.

Fox News reporter Alexandria Hoff has the latest on House Republicans questioning Smithsonian officials over claims of political bias on ‘Special Report.’ President Donald Trump's effort to root out what his administration calls "woke" ideology at the Smithsonian has grown into one of the most extensive White House reviews of the institution in decades. The Smithsonian oversees 21 museums, the National Zoo and nearly 157 million objects and specimens while receiving more than $1 billion annually in federal funding outside of private-side dollars. The administration's campaign has placed the taxpayer-supported institution at the center of a broader debate over patriotism, historical interpretation and the role of federally funded cultural institutions amid a growing divide over how people view and retell America's story. GOP LAWMAKER DEMANDS ANSWERS AFTER SMITHSONIAN CHIEF URGED MOVING BEYOND 'AMERICA FIRST MENTALITY' President Donald Trump has made reshaping the Smithsonian a priority of his broader campaign to eliminate what his administration calls "woke" ideology from federally supported institutions. (Bloomberg via Getty Images) Over the past 16 months, the administration has examined museum exhibits, educational programming, internal records and leadership statements, issued multiple document requests, interviewed curators and conducted on-site museum walkthroughs. The effort culminated in a 162-page White House report recommending sweeping reforms and announcing new executive actions aimed at implementing those recommendations. Trump signed an executive order titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" two months into his second term. The order argues that federal cultural institutions, including the Smithsonian, have promoted "divisive" ideological narratives. The executive action directs the Trump administration to restore what it describes as a more patriotic presentation of American history. And it tasks the White House Domestic Policy Council and Vice President JD Vance, in his role as a Smithsonian Regent, with reviewing Smithsonian exhibits and programs. Following Trump's executive order, the White House Domestic Policy Council kicked-off an investigation of the Smithsonian, focusing primarily on the National Museum of American History. Officials reviewed exhibits, educational materials, strategic plans, leadership speeches, museum programming and public statements. During that review, the council documented examples they argue prioritize divisive ideological narratives over a so-called patriotic telling of American history. The Smithsonian, the nation's largest museum and research complex, is at the center of a White House campaign to overhaul its presentation of American history. (J. David Ake/Getty Images) White House officials sent Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch a letter formally launching the review ordered by Trump. The letter directs the institution to turn over exhibition plans, educational materials, internal policies and other records while outlining a review of eight Smithsonian museums to ensure exhibits "celebrate American exceptionalism" and remove what the administration calls divisive narratives. It also sets deadlines for document production, curator interviews and on-site reviews, with museums instructed to begin revising public-facing content within 120 days. The Trump administration has repeatedly pressed Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch for records and changes as part of its review of the institution. (Al Drago/The Washington Post/Getty Images) The White House criticizes the museum for holding no special Independence Day programming in 2025 despite being open on July 4, discontinuing its traditional Flag Day ceremonies, and planning 250th anniversary exhibits and events. According to the administration, those 250 installations emphasize flaws of the United States while giving insufficient attention to the Founders, the Declaration of Independence and the American Revolution. The White House tells Smithsonian Secretary Bunch in a letter that the institution has failed to provide most of the records requested during its review. Among other things, the review requested exhibition plans, curatorial documents and governance materials be turned over. At this time, the administration gives the Smithsonian until Jan. 13, 2026, to produce the requested records. It also reminds the institution that federal funding must be used in a manner consistent with Trump's "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History" executive order. For Trump, the battle over the Smithsonian is part of a broader push to restore what he calls a more patriotic telling of American history across federally funded cultural institutions. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images) White House investigators complete on-site walkthroughs of Smithsonian museums. During the visits, they reviewed exhibits, educational materials, digital content and internal planning documents as well as interviewed museum staff as part of the administration's review. SMITHSONIAN'S NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AMERICAN HISTORY PROMOTES 'EXTREME POLITICAL ACTIVISM,' WH REPORT ALLEGES Investigators found during those visits exhibits that they argue emphasized restorative history, decolonization, immigration activism, DEI initiatives and social justice. Meanwhile, it claimed that the institution was downplaying America's Founders, the nation's achievements and patriotic themes. The report ultimately concludes the Smithsonian project has undergone a significant shift away from its original mission, arguing exhibits increasingly emphasize social justice activism and ideological narratives rather than focus on America's founding principles and national achievements. The White House argued the Smithsonian's flagship America 250 exhibit did not adequately celebrate the nation's Founders or the American Revolution. (Al Drago/The Washington Post/Getty Images) The museum debuts its signature exhibition commemorating America's 250th anniversary, featuring 250 objects from its collection, including Thomas Jefferson's writing desk, George Washington's uniform and the Star-Spangled Banner. The White House said just two months before the country's 250th celebration that the exhibition repackages existing displays rather than creating a new founding-era exhibit. It also criticized the installation for failing to meaningfully celebrate America's Founders, the Declaration of Independence or the American Revolution during the nation's 250th birthday. The Trump administration also said the exhibit's promotional materials and programming downplayed patriotic themes and national symbols. The White House Domestic Policy Council releases its 162-page "Saving America's Story" report, concluding that the National Museum of American History has undergone "ideological capture." The report recommends removing what it describes as political activism from museum exhibits and restoring displays that emphasize America's founding principles, national achievements and patriotic history. It says the findings stem from the Smithsonian review ordered by Trump's March 2025 executive order. The expansive report included images of exhibits, images of exhibits and placards, as well as curators and leaders of the museum. It spent much of the report focusing on how the museum classified and portrayed illegal migration in its exhibits. Hours after the report's release, Trump signs the "Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution" executive order, directing the Interior Department, Office of Management and Budget (OMB), General Services Administrator (GSA) and the White House Domestic Policy Council to use available authorities to encourage the Smithsonian to address the report's findings. TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY A photograph of President Donald Trump and a short plaque next to it are on display at the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery's "American Presidents" exhibit on Sunday, Jan. 11, 2026 in Washington. (AP Photo/Anna Johnson) Trump's order also instructs the National Park Service (NPS) to install temporary signs outside the National Museum of American History directing visitors to the report and describing the administration's concerns with the museum's presentation of American history. The administration says its effort is intended to restore a more patriotic presentation of American history at the Smithsonian. The institution, meanwhile, has long said its mission is to preserve and present the nation's history through scholarship, research and public education, setting the stage for continued debate over how America's story should be told. The Smithsonian did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. title: V.com weekend vote: What size violin did you start on? - Violinist.com
content: We have thousands of human-written stories, discussions, interviews and reviews from today through the past 20+ years. Find them here: August 3, 2026, 1:52 AM · One nice thing about violins is that they come in a lot of sizes. A four-year-old who begins piano lessons will have to wait for years until his or her hand grows large enough to reach intervals such as an octave. But a four-year-old can comfortably navigate a 1/16-size violin. Smaller violins have been around for hundreds of years, and even Stradivari was thought to have made a few violins that would be considered 3/4-size today. Starting as young as he did, Mozart had a fractional violin - but this was a rarity in the 18th century. Fractional violins became more common -- and more standardized -- in the last century, especially with the advent of the Suzuki method, with its emphasis on early childhood learning. Of course, if you started as an adult, you likely started on a full-size violin. But not necessarily! A petite-size adult might choose a smaller violin. It's been a while since I was a beginner, but I recall starting on a 1/2-size violin, just shy of my ninth birthday. What size violin did you start on? If you started super-young you can't vote for a "Cracker-Jack box" but you can mention it in the comments, as well as your age! August 3, 2026 at 09:58 AM · I started learning the violin at age 60 on a full size violin... which was a mistake. I'm a very petite woman and within a year I'd traded in my first violin for a 7/8 which fit me so much better. It's a pity the local violin shop didn't advise me to start on a smaller violin from the beginning. (BTW, I already played a wind instrument and the piano or else it would have been an even more mammoth task!) August 3, 2026 at 10:10 AM · I'm fairly certain I started on a 1/2 size, as I was quite a tall kid. I changed quickly between 3/4 and 4/4 violins. August 3, 2026 at 12:42 PM · I have no recollection.  Probably a 1/2 size.  One of my teachers showed me the 1/32 size violin he started on. August 3, 2026 at 01:01 PM · I started in 4th grade in 1965 on a full sized violin owned by my family. I had public school group lessons, and I don't think anyone had a fractional sized violin. At least, I don't remember mine being weirdly large! August 3, 2026 at 01:44 PM · Full size. I was already at least 19 years old, the first time. (I quit by the time I was 26 and I wish I’d kept going) August 3, 2026 at 02:05 PM · Full-size - I started at 58. August 4, 2026 at 12:44 AM · I was 7 and started on a 1/8 size. Mom had bought a decent 1/4 size from China online that my relatives brought over since she saw online 1/4 was average for a 7-year-old. title: Jim Valvano: Jimmy V Foundation honors cancer research and resilience for patients with wine celebration held in Napa Valley - ABC7 Bay Area
content: In Napa Valley, V Foundation recognized scientists advancing cancer research and patients whose lives have been affected by cancer NAPA, Calif.  (KGO) -- Nearly 40% of people will be diagnosed with cancer, according to the National Cancer Institute, a statistic that highlights the importance of research efforts aimed at improving treatments and finding cures. In Napa Valley on Saturday night, the V Foundation recognized both scientists advancing cancer research and patients whose lives have been affected by the disease with the V Foundation Wine Celebration. For Harper Harrell and her family, the impact of cancer became personal when she was diagnosed with leukemia at age 8. "Hearing that your child has cancer is like a nightmare, right? It's it's your worst fears confirmed," said her mother, Heather Hindin. Harrell underwent two and a half years of treatment. "I remember it just being all a blur. It really was such a scary time," said Harrell, now 13. Despite the challenges, her family said she focused on helping others. Harrell raised more than $27,000 for the V Foundation while undergoing treatment and overcoming cancer herself. "We've really been able to find our purpose through this journey. And it makes me just extremely proud of her," Hilton said. The V Foundation traces its roots to a speech delivered by former basketball coach Jim Valvano at the ESPY Awards in 1993, during which he urged people: "Don't give up. Don't ever give up." Those words continue to resonate with ESPN college basketball analyst Jay Bilas, a member of the foundation's board. "Every year that speech is replayed and there's always new audiences for it, and they're always moved the same way that we were moved some 33 years ago by his speech," Bilas said. The foundation provides grants each year to young scientists to support research projects that might otherwise go unfunded. "You need two things to be successful in science. You need a great idea, and you need money to execute that great idea," said Dr. Barry Sleckman of the V Foundation Scientific Advisory Committee. Valvano said research could not save him but expressed hope that it would help future generations. Today it's doing just that. "It was hard, very, very hard. But, if it didn't happen, we wouldn't be here being able to speak for the kids who can't be here and who need the research," Harrell said. Mark Joseph Tenerowicz. M-A-R-K J-O-S-E-P-H T-E-N-E-R-O-W- I-C-Z. I was an emergency physician. I'm currently not acting as an emergency physician. Directing your attention to January 24th, 2023, were you working in the evening hours that day? And at some point in time, did you treat a child named Dawson Clancy? And when he arrived, were you given a summary of his injuries by emergency personnel? I was told that he reportedly had been strangled and he was found without a pulse and not breathing. CPR was in progress. He was not breathing on his own and he had no pulse in him, was not responding. And after ... Well, strike that. Did you observe any trauma to his body? He was a native of Montgomery County and grew up in Uvalda. He was a 1976 graduate of Montgomery County High School and has lived in Vidalia since 1979. He was known as an excellent carpenter, working early in his career with Lake McDonald Construction and later as a superintendent for Harry Moses Construction. He also worked with Copper Construction, but was self-employed the last several years before his retirement. Stanley was a Christian and loved the Lord and was a member of Cedar Crossing Baptist Church. He was an outdoorsman, enjoying quail and deer hunting, fishing at Dead River and the Altamaha, and woodworking, making a variety of things, including birdhouses and wells. Above all, he cherished the time he spent with his granddaughter. He is preceded in death by his parents, Homer Douglas Poole and Jeanette King Poole. Koleci, 88, of Albany and Cleverdale, New York, passed away peacefully on August 2, 2026, after a courageous battle with illness, surrounded by his loving family. Tom is survived by his devoted wife of 56 years, Stella Koleci; his son, Vasil Koleci; his daughters, Dr. Carolann Koleci and Dr. Nicole Rosa (Todd); and his brother, Lewis Koleci. He is also survived by his three cherished grandchildren, John, Sophia, and Alexis Quackenbush, as well as several loving nieces, nephews, and many cherished friends. He was predeceased by his beloved parents, Proxethea and Vasil Koleci. Thomas possessed a deep, lifelong love of learning. He attended Hudson Valley Technical Institute before beginning a distinguished 37-year career as a mechanical and plumbing engineer with the New York State Office of General Services. Throughout his career, he designed plumbing and steam systems for many major New York State buildings and facilities. He found great satisfaction in tackling challenging engineering projects and seeing them through to completion. Above all, Thomas cherished his family. He loved spending weekends boating on Lake George, camping, and enjoying the beauty of the Adirondacks with those he loved most. He was a founding member of the Harris Bay Yacht Club following its transition from the Yardarm, and he treasured the friendships and memories made there over the years. A devoted member of St. Sophia Greek Orthodox Church, Thomas's faith was the cornerstone of his life. His commitment to his church and community reflected the kindness, humility, and generosity with which he lived each day. Music brought him immense joy throughout his life. An accomplished trumpet player, he performed with a local dance band and instilled a love of music in his family. He never missed an opportunity to attend his children's and grandchildren's band concerts, always cheering them on with pride. Thomas had an inquisitive mind and a passion for science, engineering, and lifelong learning. He loved home improvement and automotive projects and was known by family and friends as someone who could fix almost anything. One of his greatest pleasures was passing along his knowledge, practical skills, and love of engineering to his son. He also made Christmas a magical time for his family, creating traditions and memories that will be treasured for generations. With his sharp intellect, he delighted in quickly completing the Sunday crossword puzzle, often finishing it before anyone else had a chance. Thomas will be remembered for his unwavering work ethic, brilliant mind, steadfast faith, musical spirit, and deep love for his family. His legacy lives on in the lives he touched and the values he instilled in those who knew and loved him. title: Is Chelsea v Tottenham on TV? Channel, kick-off time and how to watch preseason friendly - Yahoo Sports
content: Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur continue their preparations for the new Premier League season as the two London clubs meet in Sydney. In the wake of the World Cup, both Xabi Alonso and Roberto De Zerbi are using their preseason tour to look at the depth of two growing squads, with Chelsea continuing to pursue a number of transfer targets and Spurs significantly strengthened already this summer. This game will offer another opportunity to get minutes in the legs with just a few weeks to go until the campaign proper starts. Each has already achieved a win over local opposition and another good crowd is likely as Australia-based fans enjoy a rare chance to see their team in person. Chelsea vs Tottenham is due to kick off at 10.45am BST on Saturday 1 August at the Accor Stadium in Sydney. A live stream will be available to subscribers to CFC+ or SPURSPLAY, the club's respective in-house streaming homes. Xabi Alonso was pleased to get through a 10-goal game against Western Sydney Wanderers with no fresh injury concerns, and may be able to utilise Romeo Lavia, who missed that game with a hamstring niggle. Maxence Lacroix may have to wait for a first outing at his new club. Mateus Fernandes will miss out again for Tottenham as a cautious approach is taken with a calf complaint. Roberto De Zerbi is likely to rotate, while Kevin Danso, Micky Van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke could have some involvement after their World Cup exertions.
